connections.feedback: No tool always gives the one correct answer. AI can be useful and still be wrong, so you check what matters.
AI cannot know what people are thinking. It can help you word a question to them, but it cannot read their minds.
AI can offer ideas or lists, but a personal matter is yours to decide. It does not know your life or what matters to you.
AI is good at turning rough points into a first draft. You still read it and change it, but it saves a lot of starting effort.

This says the topic, the kind of help (a simple explanation) and what to do next (practice questions). Clear requests get more useful answers.
This names the topic and a task, which is fine. It leaves out your level and what to do next, so a fuller request would serve you better.
connections.notes: Ambiguous: clear enough to work, weaker than the strong choice.

connections.feedback: One word does not tell the tool what you want. It could define water, describe a lake or anything else. Say the topic and the help you need.

The tone you want is safe and useful to include. It helps the tool write in the right voice.
The topic is the point of your request. It is safe to include and needed to get a useful answer.

connections.feedback: Sounding sure is not proof. AI tools can state wrong details just as confidently as right ones.
Opening hours can change, and AI may repeat old or wrong information. The library's own website or phone line is the reliable place to check.
Repeating the question to the same tool is not a check. It can repeat the same mistake. Use a different, trusted source.

A library's own site or phone line is the reliable source for its hours. Use that before you travel.
For a student with time to spare, a wasted trip is a small cost, so going anyway is understandable. Checking first is still the better habit.
connections.notes: Ambiguous: low stakes make this defensible.

connections.feedback: A confident tone does not make the hours correct. Opening times change, so check with the library itself before you travel.

AI tools make text that sounds natural, but they can be wrong. That is why checking matters.

You chose to send the letter, so its content is yours. Read what AI writes before you send it.
A tool cannot take responsibility. The person who uses and sends the words does.
The reader is not responsible for catching your mistakes. The sender is, and reading before sending is the way to catch them.

connections.feedback: You can tell the tool what to change, such as 'make it shorter'. Refining a result step by step is normal.
Editing it yourself works, and keeps you in control. The point of this question, though, is that you can ask the tool to revise.

connections.feedback: You can ask the tool to revise its work, and it will usually try again. Tell it what to change, such as 'make it shorter'.
A tiny font makes a poster hard to read. Change the content instead, and ask the tool to shorten the paragraph.

connections.feedback: AI can explain hard text in simpler words. Reading the paragraph again afterward is how you actually learn it.
Copying without reading means you do not know whether it is right or whether it answers the assignment.
Skipping the reading means skipping the learning, and the tool may leave out important parts. Ask for an explanation, then read.
Handing in work you did not do is dishonest. Use AI to help you learn, then do the work yourself.

Telling a beginner to share everything is unsafe. Good teaching includes keeping private details out.
A long manual read alone can feel overwhelming. Practice with a friendly guide helps more.
This makes your friend more nervous and is not true. Many people start with simple tasks.

Giving AI your notes keeps the content yours, and the tool does the sorting. Comparing the list with your notes catches anything it dropped.
The tool does not know your family's needs. Decisions about people should include them.
Using the list without comparing it to your notes means a missing item goes unnoticed.

connections.notes: Ambiguous: courteous, but unnecessary if the number is simply left out.

connections.feedback: AI can help with the words, and you can add the number yourself at the end. That keeps another person's details out of the request.
More detail about a person does not mean a better answer. Share only what the task needs, and keep others' details out.
The number is someone else's private detail. It does not make the message better, so leave it out.

connections.feedback: Your doubt is a good signal. Compare the recipe with a trusted one before you cook, because AI can write steps that sound normal but are wrong.
Following a step you doubt without checking could waste ingredients or spoil the dish. Look into it first.
If the same tool gives the same time again, that is not proof. It may repeat the same mistake.
A clear, confident recipe can still contain a wrong time. When something looks odd, trust your doubt and check.

connections.feedback: A tool does not necessarily look things up. Many answers come from patterns in text it learned.
Confidence and correctness are different things. Wrong answers can sound just as sure.
A confident tone is just how the text is written. It says nothing about whether the content is true.
Nobody has confirmed an answer just because it is written confidently. Confidence is a style, so look for real evidence.
